Memory Jogger.new: Alaska sold state timber on condition that buyers process it in Alaska before export; the Court held that a parallel federal-lands policy was not ``unmistakably clear'' congressional authorization, and a plurality held that the market-participant exception does not let a State impose conditions that regulate a downstream market it does not participate in (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/467/82/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court \textbf{reversed and remanded} the Ninth Circuit by a \textbf{6--2} vote, with one Justice not participating. The case was argued on February 29, 1984, and decided on May 22, 1984 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/467/82/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/467/82}{Cornell LII}):

Analysis of Opinions.src: First, Part~II's six-Justice majority cemented the ``unmistakably clear'' canon for congressional authorization of state trade barriers, relied upon in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/477/131/}{\textit{Maine v.\ Taylor}}, 477 U.S.\ 131, 138--139 (1986) (rejecting implied consent under the Lacey Act), and contrasted with express statutory authorization in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/472/159/}{\textit{Northeast Bancorp, Inc.\ v.\ Board of Governors}}, 472 U.S.\ 159 (1985).

Analysis of Opinions.new: \item \textbf{The Downstream Limit in Later Market-Participant Cases:}

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Invalid Downstream Mandate): In-State Refining of State-Land Lithium.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: Nevada auctions state-land lithium leases requiring winning bidders to refine all extracted lithium at in-state facilities before export, invoking a federal statute requiring domestic processing of \emph{federal}-land minerals. Under \textit{Wunnicke} Part~II, parallel federal-land policy is not ``unmistakably clear'' authorization. Under Part~III, Nevada participates in raw-lithium leasing, not downstream refining; imposing post-extraction processing strings on a natural resource entering foreign trade fails market-participant immunity and is virtually \textit{per se} invalid under \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/397/137/}{\textit{Pike v.\ Bruce Church, Inc.}}, 397 U.S.\ 137 (1970).

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Invalid Downstream Mandate): Resale Restrictions on State-Made Cement.} A State that operates its own cement plant sells cement to private distributors on condition that they resell it only to customers within the State, even after title and payment have passed. Out-of-state builders who would buy from the distributors challenge the condition. The State may choose its own customers, as \textit{Reeves} allowed, but here it reaches past its sale to control the buyers' later dealings in a resale market where the State is not a participant. The plurality identified exactly this kind of post-sale restriction as one of the features absent from \textit{Reeves}, and a resale ban that walls off the State's market for local benefit is the kind of downstream regulation \textit{Wunnicke} forbids.
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Valid Market Participation): A State-Owned Refinery Choosing Its Customers.} Return to the lithium hypothetical, but suppose Nevada instead

Examples: Future Applications.src: operates a state-owned refinery and sells refined lithium exclusively to Nevada battery makers during shortages

Examples: Future Applications.new: . Nevada is now acting as a seller in the very market it has entered and is simply choosing its customers, the conduct \textit{Reeves} protected when South Dakota sold cement from its own plant to residents first. No condition follows the lithium after sale into a market Nevada does not participate in, so the market-participant exception applies and the Dormant Commerce Clause does not bar the preference.
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Valid Market Participation): Cash Subsidies Instead of Export Conditions.} Alternatively, suppose Nevada

Examples: Future Applications.src: auctions raw leases without export conditions while paying direct general-fund cash subsidies to in-state refiners

Examples: Future Applications.new: . Lessees remain free to ship raw ore anywhere, so the State has not stripped buyers of their choice, the feature that distinguished \textit{Alexandria Scrap} from Alaska's contract clause. The subsidy may favor local refiners, but a direct payment from the State's own funds is not a regulation of the downstream market, and the plurality noted that such alternatives remain open to a State.

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Close Call): Requiring Resident Logging Crews on State Land.} Alaska sells standing timber on state land and requires that the buyer use crews made up of Alaska residents to cut and haul the timber off state land; once the logs leave state land, the buyer may process and ship them anywhere. Alaska argues that, as in \textit{White}, the workers are effectively working on a state project before the sale is complete. The challenger replies that the condition regulates the separate labor market for logging services. Because the plurality defined the market by intuition without an objective test, and because Part~III never commanded a majority, it is unclear whether harvesting on state land falls inside the timber-sales market or downstream of it.

Key Quotations.src: ``There is no talismanic significance to the phrase `expressly stated,' however; it merely states one way of meeting the requirement that, for a state regulation to be removed from the reach of the dormant Commerce Clause, congressional intent must be unmistakably clear. The requirement that Congress affirmatively contemplate otherwise invalid state legislation is mandated by the policies underlying dormant Commerce Clause doctrine.''

``The fact that the state policy in this case appears to be consistent with federal policy---or even that state policy furthers the goals we might believe that Congress had in mind---is an insufficient indicium of congressional intent. Congress acted only with respect to federal lands; we cannot infer from that fact that it intended to authorize a similar policy with respect to state lands.''

``The limit of the market participant doctrine must be that it allows a State to impose burdens on commerce within the market in which it is a participant, but allows it to go no further. The State may not impose conditions, whether by statute, regulation, or contract, that have a substantial regulatory effect outside of that particular market. Unless the `market' is relatively narrowly defined, the doctrine has the potential of swallowing up the rule that States may not impose substantial burdens on interstate commerce even if they act with the permissible state purpose of fostering local industry.''
Justice White (plurality opinion), \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/467/82/}{467 U.S.\ at 97--98} (\href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/467/82}{Cornell LII})

``Alaska is merely paying the buyer of the timber indirectly, by means of a reduced price, to hire Alaska residents to process the timber. Under existing precedent, the State could accomplish that same result in any number of ways. \dots\ It seems to me unduly formalistic to conclude that the one path chosen by the State as best suited to promote its concerns is the path forbidden it by the Commerce Clause.''
